items.title: No outcome independent of the feedback system
items.whyItMatters: The retrieved trial measured its primary outcome with the feedback system itself, and staff can satisfy the badge without cleaning their hands (claims c1, c6).
items.opportunity: Use direct observation by external observers, equally visible on both arms, as the primary outcome.

items.title: Contamination through float staff
items.whyItMatters: One in five nursing shifts is worked by float staff, who shrank a between-arm difference by a third in a similar trial (claim c5).
items.opportunity: Randomise pairs of wards that share staff and record float status at every observed opportunity.

items.title: Infection outcomes cannot be compared in six months
items.whyItMatters: About three events a month in a whole hospital cannot show a ward-level difference.
items.opportunity: Report infections descriptively as context, not as an effect estimate.

items.title: Staff trust in the monitoring agreement
items.whyItMatters: Feedback that feels like surveillance may fall hardest on float staff, agency staff and junior doctors, who have least control over their workload.
items.opportunity: Keep data at ward level, involve staff representatives, and report acceptability by staff group.

items.title: Local effect size is uncertain
items.whyItMatters: The only trial reports a large effect on a system-measured outcome and a smaller one on observation.
items.opportunity: State the smallest difference the board would pay for before sample size is fixed.

errorsFound: The vendor's claim rests on the feedback system's own compliance figure, which the feedback itself can move without changing hand hygiene.
reevaluation: The gaps point to a cluster randomised trial of paired wards with an independent observed primary outcome, and to honesty about what infection counts can show.
summary: Five gaps; outcome independence and contamination are high severity.
